**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Geography 2 (0750), Paper 2, ADVANCED LEVEL, JUNE 2023. Duration: THREE HOURS.**

Instructions to candidates: Answer FOUR questions, choosing at least ONE from each Section.

All questions carry twenty-five marks each. You are encouraged to refer to specific examples drawn from any part of the world. Credit will be given for such specific examples.

Only the required number of questions will be marked.

Marks will be awarded for well annotated maps and diagrams where these are relevant.

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(a) Examine FOUR measures to solve the problems associated with ageing population.

(9 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
An **ageing population** is one in which the proportion of old people (65 years and over) is rising and that of the young and of the working-age group is falling, as a result of low birth rates and rising life expectancy (Japan, Germany, Italy, Sweden and many countries of Europe and East Asia). Its problems are a **high dependency ratio** (fewer workers supporting more retired people), the rising cost of pensions and health care, a shortage of labour, lower tax income and the need for housing and care for the elderly. Four measures to solve them are the following.

1. **Increase the retirement age and encourage older people to remain in work.** Raising the age at which pensions are paid, introducing flexible and part-time employment, retraining and the ending of age discrimination lengthen the working life, increase the tax and contribution income, and reduce the number of years in which pensions are paid (reforms in the United Kingdom, Germany and France).
2. **Reform pensions and social security.** Governments can require workers to contribute to private or occupational pension funds and encourage savings, so that the cost is not carried only by the working-age population through taxes; contributions and benefits are reviewed regularly.
3. **Encourage births (pro-natalist policies) and the employment of women.** Child allowances, tax reductions, paid maternity and paternity leave, cheap child care and housing support (France, Sweden, Singapore) raise the birth rate and the future labour force, and facilities for working mothers raise the number of workers.
4. **Encourage immigration of young workers.** Admitting young migrants fills labour shortages, adds to the contributions and gives a younger age structure, as in Germany and Canada. This must be done with integration policies to avoid social tension.

Other measures include **health and care services** for the elderly (preventive medicine, community care, retirement homes, long-term care insurance), which keep the old people healthy and independent for longer, and the use of **technology** and automation (robots in Japan) to compensate for the shortage of labour.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(b) Briefly explain how and why migration is sex selective.

(10 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Migration is sex selective** when the migrants are not equally men and women, so that one sex is more strongly represented among the migrants than in the population as a whole. The proportion depends on the type of migration and the region.

**How migration is sex selective.**

- In many developing countries in **Africa and South Asia**, **young men** predominate in rural-urban and international labour migration (to the cities, mines, plantations and oil-producing countries, and to Europe and the Gulf), so that the rural areas are left with a surplus of women, children and the elderly, and the towns have an excess of males.
- In **Latin America, South-East Asia and the Caribbean**, in contrast, **young women** predominate among rural-urban migrants (domestic work, factories, services) and among international migrants who become nurses, care workers, domestic and hotel workers, as in the case of the Philippines.
- In **refugee flows**, men often leave first, or are killed or forced to stay, and women and children are the majority in the camps; in **marriage migration**, women usually move to the home of the husband.

**Why migration is sex selective.**

1. **Type of jobs available (economic reasons).** Mining, construction, plantation, transport and heavy industry attract men, while textile and electronic factories, domestic and care work, nursing, retailing and the services attract women, so that the employment opportunities of the destination decide who goes.
2. **Social and cultural factors.** In patriarchal societies women are expected to stay at home, look after the children and the elderly and work on the family farm, they inherit little land and are less likely to be allowed to travel alone, whereas the men are expected to provide for the family and to migrate. In other societies, women have greater access to paid work in the towns and migrate in larger numbers.
3. **Level of education and gender equality.** Better-educated women and women with more independence have more opportunity to migrate for study or employment.
4. **Risk, cost and physical demands of the journey.** Long, dangerous and expensive journeys favour men, who are assumed to be more mobile and able to take risks, while women with young children migrate less often.
5. **Family and marriage.** Women move at marriage (or to join their husbands under family reunification), and men often migrate first and send for the family later. Wars and conflicts, and government policies that restrict the entry of certain categories of people, also affect the sex ratio.

**Consequences** include an unbalanced sex ratio in the source and destination areas, with changes in fertility, marriage patterns and the roles of women in the villages left by the men.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(c) Discuss THREE significance of the Demographic Transition Model.

(7 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
The **Demographic Transition Model (DTM)** shows how the birth rate, the death rate and so the natural increase of a population change over time as a country develops, in four (or five) stages: stage 1 (high stationary: high birth and death rates), stage 2 (early expanding: death rate falls, birth rate stays high), stage 3 (late expanding: birth rate falls) and stage 4 (low stationary: low birth and death rates), with a possible stage 5 (declining or ageing population).

![fig-1](gce-al-geography-2023-p2-officiel-cameroun_exercice_4_fig_1.png)

Its significance (importance) is as follows.

1. **It explains population change and growth.** It shows that the rapid growth of population (population explosion) is due to the gap between the high birth rate and the falling death rate in stage 2, which is caused by better health care, sanitation, food supply and medicine. It also shows why growth slows down in stage 3, because of urbanisation, education, family planning and the greater status of women, so that it helps to understand the changes in population size.
2. **It links population change to levels of development and allows the comparison of countries.** Countries can be placed in a stage and compared: for example, the United Kingdom and Japan are in a late stage with low growth or decline, while many countries of sub-Saharan Africa, including Cameroon, are in stage 2 or the beginning of stage 3 with high growth and a young population.
3. **It is useful for planning and for forecasting.** Governments can use the model to predict the future size and age structure of the population and to plan the services needed: schools, maternity care and jobs in the expanding stages; pensions, health care and housing for the aged in the late stages; and population policies (family planning or birth promotion).

**Limitations** (for balance): the model is based on the experience of European countries, so that not all countries follow its sequence or time scale; it ignores migration and the effect of wars, epidemics (such as HIV/AIDS) and government policies, and it does not explain the exact causes of the fall in the birth rate. In spite of these limits it remains a basic tool in population geography.
